entries.title: 2TH 2:8
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content: -Importance of re'ligious know7edge. We are surrounded by m1my l11H11ences tending either to lead us into e1Tor and delusion, or into scepticism and infidolity. We must add to our faith knowledge, and seek to be rooted and grounded in the faith. The truth ought to be the great ~ubject of inquiry. Let us cultivate the love of the truth; let us pursue the truth wherever it leads, lest we should render ourselves liable to the condemnation of those who believe not the truth, but hnve pleasure in un- rigbteonsness; and lest we should be led from error to error, and be lost in a perfeot maz1:1 of falsehood.

entries.title: 2TH 2:8–9
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content: -f'M doctrine of antichmt. Antichrist is the caricature or counterpart of Christ.. 1. He is the man of sin, the personification of iniquity; whereas Christ is the righteous One, the personification of righteousness. 2. He is the rpystery of iniquity; whereas Christ is the mystery of godliness. 8. His advent is announced hy the s"me word as the advent of Christ. 4. His coming occurred in its proper season; ~o also Christ came in the fulness of time. 5. His coming is after the working of Satan; whereas Christ's coming is in the power of the Hoiy Ghost. 6. He performR miracles of falsehood, a counterpart of the real miracles which Christ performed. 7. He sitteth in the temple of God, thus occupdng the proper seat of Christ. 8. He ,hows or exhibits himself as God, whereas Christ is the true manifestation of the Gorlhead. In short, the king,lom of light which Christ has established has its counterpart in the kingdom of darkne ,.

entries.title: 2TH 2:13
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content: -Sanctijication. 1. Its nature. It denotes separation and consecration. It consists in the mortification of sin and the production of holiness. 2. Its properties. Universal, adapted to our peculiar characters, discernible, progressive, in this life always imperfect, constant, and eternal. 3. lts Author. The Holy Spirit the immediate Anthor; it is his peculiar office to produce holiness in the soul. He not only purifies our affections, but takes up his abode in our hearts. 4. lts instrument. The belief.of the truth. The instrument with which the Spirit works is the Word of God. We must not disjoin these two; the agency of the Spirit and the instrumentality of the Word arc both equally essential and equally important.

entries.title: 2TH 2:15
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content: -Retention of Scripture. Whilst we reject the false and wrong, we mus hold fast to the true and right. This is an age of testing. 1. We must examine the evidences of the Word of God. 2. We must endeavour to find out its meaning b,· careful study, and by prayer for the guidance and teaching of God's Spirit. 3. \\" e must bring all doctrines and opinions to the test of Scripture, and draw our belief fro111 the Word of God. and not from the opinions and traditions of men. 4. We must ever walk up to the light which we have. The Spirit is promised to guide us into all truth, and if we depend upon him and follow bis guidance, we shall not he 11utrered to go astray

entries.title: 2TH 2:3–8
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content:
-The rise of the apostasy and the revelation of the man of ain must precede the second advent. This fact would assure them that a period of time of at least indefinite extent would intervene before the day of the Lord. "Let no man deceive you by any means." I. THE COMmG OF THE APOSTASY, "Because the day will not set in nnless there come the apostasy first." I. The apostasy is so described because it was already familiar to their minds through his oral teaching. "Remember ye not, that, when I was with you, I was telling you of these things?" 2. lt points to a signal defection from the Christian faith. We imagine that the primitive Churches were signally free from error or fault of any sort. 'l'he apostle himself notes the signs of beginning apostasy even in his own day. (1) "The mystery of lawlessness d!)th already work." (2) There were for himself "pcrib from false brethren." (3) There were in the Chw·ch itself "enemies of the cross of Christ." (4) Later still "many deceivers had entere, 1 into the world." (5) The apostle foresaw that the evil "would increase unto more ungodliness." (6) '!'bis apostasy was to prec,·de the revelation of the man of sin, not to be regarded as identical with it. Yet the two movements were not to be regarded as independent of each other, except in the order or time of their development. (7) The signs of the apostasy in Christendom are to be seen principally in the Papacy, but likewise in the kindred errors and corruptions of the Greek Church as well as in the delusions of Mohammedanism. The elements of the apostasy were, however, to be gathered up and concentrated at last in a single person 118 their final embodiment. II. 'l'nE REVELATION OF TIIE MAN Oll' BIN, •• And that man of ·sin be revealed, the son of perdition; who opposeth and exalteth himself above every one called God, or an object of worship." His characteristics are here distinctly dcscri lied. I. He does not represent a system of error, like Romanism, or the papal hierarcl,y, or a succession of popes, but a single person. The man of sin has not yet appeared. Yet Homanism, or the papacy, comprehends much that is invoh·ed in the idea of this terrible person, who, however, goes beyond it in the appalling extent of his wickedness. The passage is not symbolic, but literal. It is a liternl person who is described. 2. He is Othe son of perdition." (1) Not because he brings ruin to others, but (2) because he is himself doomed to ruin-going liternlly to "his own place," like Judas, who may he regarded as a type of him. 3. His boundless and blasphemous assunq,tions. (1) Hi■ opposition to evory God, true and false. (2) His self-elevation above every Uod, true and false. His action recalls the prophecy of Daniel : "The king shall do according to his will ; and he shall exalt himself above every god, and shall speak marvellous things against the God of gods" (Dan. xi, 36). This prophecy refers to a polytheistic king. The apostle refen to Uie man of sin 118 repudiating all worship, u ii he represented a higher divinity ,IMm anything worshipped <a earlh. (a) 'fto SO THE SECOND EPISTLE TO 'l'HE 'l'HESSALONIANS. [oH. u. 1-17.

,l<'l!cription does not apply to the pope or the papacy: (a) Because the pope, though the hP.ad or a syst.c-m of idolatry, does not oppose God or exRlt hims .. lf ahove him but rather owns himself " e. servant of servants of the most high God," and blesses the people, not in his own name, but in the Name of the Triune God. (.S) Because instead of exalting himself above God or objects of worship, he multiplies the objects 'or worship by the canonization of new saints, and submits, like the humblest of his followers to the worship of the very saints he has made. ('I') Because the pope, though guilty of Rrrogating almost Dil'ine powers to himself, does not supersede God so I\S to make himself God. The man of sin "sitteth in the temple of God, showing himself that he is God." Though votaries of the papacy have often given Divine titles to the popes, the Popes have never assumed to be God, but only vicars of Jesus Christ on earth. They ha"c clRimcd t.o be viceroys of God. The temple of God cannot be the Vatican• nor the Christian Church, which is an ideal building; nor can Rorue be regarded as th~ centre of the Christian Church. (5) Because this prophetic sketch contains no allusion to strictly papal peculiarities, such as idolatry, either as to the Virgin Mary, saints angels, or relics, the invention of purgatory, priestly absolution, bloody fanaticism' <lebased casuistry, lordship over the world of spirit.~. (b) The description applies ~ the man of sin-the lawless one-for whom the Papacy prepares the way by a Iona course of apostnsy from the truth. (a) Thie terrible person is t.o oppose God and ali worship of every sort, and may therefore be regarded as an impersonation of infidel wickedness. (,8) He is t.o sit down in the vaoated "temple of God'' and claim all the attributes of divinity. He sits down in God's place-for the temple is God's dwelling~ iu some actual temple, and appropriates it to his own use. Wherever the scene of thiff marvellons usurpation may be, it signifies the obliteration of all Christian interests and the triumph of atheistic malignity. When the Lord comes, 11 shall he find faith in the earth?" We see how Positivism in our own day has forsaken the worship of a personal God and betaken itself to the worship of concrete humanity. The man of Bin will use the papacy as Auguste Comte travestied it in constructing forms of Posi- tivist devotion, by turning it into some darker shape and making it the tremendous instrument of the world's final ruin. Ill. THE CHECK TO TJIE FULL DEVELOPMENT OF THE MAN 01!' SIN. "And now what restmineth ye know, in order that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of iniquity is already working only till he who now restraineth be taken out of the way." These words imply: 1. That the apostasy was already in being; for" the mystery of lawlessness is already working." The two, if not identical, are closely connected together. (1) It antagonizes Christ, who is "the mystery of godliness" (1 Tim. iii. 16). The mystery is a process, not a person, yet it works against the person of Christ. (2) Many of the elements of the "apostasy" were in existence in the days of the apostles, at least in the germ-state. The Epistle to the Colossians and the Second Epistle to Timothy point to an early development of Gnostic error which found its place in due time in the papal system (Col. ii.; 2 Tim. iii.). The self-deifying 1endency was manifested in the conduct of several of the Cresars. 2. The words imply that the working of the apostasy was still undefined and as yet unguessed at. It was still "a mystery," t.o be revealed in due time. Nothing is more remarkable than the gradual growth of error in the patristic age. False opinions held by pious Fathers in one age were held by errorists in the next age to the exclusion ot the truth. 3. The word, imply that, a, the apostasy t0ou1d last through ages, the check would likewise exercise a continuous effect. The common opinion is that the Roman empire was the restraining power upon the development of the man of sin. It was certainly such upon the course of the apostasy, which was to prepare the way for the man of sin. It held the Papacy in check till it was itself swept away by barbarian violence. B1icause it has passed away, it does not follow that the man of sin must have been revealed at once; for other checks have been supplied, and ue being still continuously supplied, in the polity of nations and in the face of Divine truth, to restrain the last terrible manifestation of his power. IV. THE 00011 OF THE !UN or sor. "Whom the Lord Jeaus shall consume with the breath of bis mouth, aud shall destroy with the appearance of his coming." I. Thia d- Mt ,.ifer to the Word and Spirit of Chrut working in tlu minds of men for the , / ~ of untichristi.an error and antithei,tic wickedneRs. but to the aclual oa. 11. 1-17.] 'fHE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONlANS. 31

versonal advent of Juus (Jhriat. 2. TM language implies the suddennesa and the completeness of th• overthrow of the man of sin, who th,reby becomes "the 80'n of perdition." 3, The picture presented may be identical with the Gog and Magog conspiracy wliich i, to follow th. millennium. (Rev, xx. 7, 8.) The Lord puts the question, "When the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith in the earth?" (Luke xviii. 8). 'l.'hus the apostle assures the Thessalonians that the day of the Lord cannot have come, because all the events here pictured ml18t happen before that great and terrible day.-T. C.

entries.title: 2TH 2:9–12
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content:
-The methods of the man of Bin and the retribution that overtaku hi, victims. The apostle, after telling the doom of the man of sin by anticipation, goes back upon his description so as to bring out the contrast between the coming of Christ and the coming of his arch-enemy. I. THE METHODS OF THE MAN OF BIN, "Whose coming is after the working of Satan in all powers and signs and prodigies of lying." 1. The sau1·ce of all this wonderworking activity-Satan. There is more than human depravity at work in this tremendol18 revelation of evil power. As Satan is a liar and the rather of lies, he will stamp falsehood upon the whole system, which he will elaborate with superhuman oraft for the misguidance of ir.en. 2. The character of this activity. It is external and internal. (1) It is external-" in powers and signs and prodigies of lying." (a) These are to be a mimicry of Christ's miracles, for the three words here used are twice applied to our Lord's miracles (Heb. ii. 4; Acts ii. 22). (b) They were not real miracles, as if they had been done by Divine power, but jugglers' tricks or such-like startling wonders as might delude " the perishing" into the belief that they were done by Divine power. The signs were to be as false as their author. (c) Their design was to attest the truth of the doctrine of the man of sin. (2) It is internal-" in all deceit of unrighteousness "-so as to pass sooner for truth. Guile marks his whole career, and unrighteousness is the aim and result. He " speaks lies in hypocrisy ; " "by good words and fair speeches ho deceives the hearts of the simple" (1 Tim. iv. 2; Rom. xvi. 18). 'l.'he ministc,rs of Satan can as easily transform themselves into ministers of righteousness as Satan himself become an" angel of light" (2 Cor. xi. 14, 15). 3. The effects of this wonder-working activity. They are confined "to those tbat are perishing." It is not possible " to deceive the elect" (Mark xiii. 22). Those who are blinded to the glory of the gospel are in the way of easy deception (2 Cor. iv. 3). It is those on the way to perdition who are so easily deceived. II. THE RETRlllUTION THAT OVERTAKES THE VICTIMS OF THE MAN OF SIN, .. Because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved." The causes of the success of the man of sin are first described on the side of man and then on the side of God. The whole case is one of just retribution. 1. The sin of the perishing. (1) The truth was that which brought salve.lion near, disclosing at once their need of a Saviour and the readiness of Christ to save them. (2) They did not receive it, though it was offered them, but rejected and despised it. (3) 'l'hey rejected it because they had "not the love of the truth." Without this love, the truth will do us no good; it must be received into the heart as well as the head. Augustine prayed, "Lord, make me taste that by love which I taste by knowledge." 2. The Divine retrib1<tionfor th. Bin of th. perishing. "And for this cause God is sending them an inworking error, that they should believe the lie" of the man of sin. They rejected the truth of God; God will, as a judicial, punitive infliction, send them blindness so that the error of the man of sin will be received as truth. "A terrible combination when both God and Satan are agreed to deceive a man!" There is a double punishment here. (1) They will actually believe the lie of the man Jf sin. Sin often in the moral government of God is punished by deeper sin. Those who care nothing for the truth are easily seduced into the worst errors. Men will at last become so perverse as to call " evil good, and good evil." (2) They wiU be finally judged for the pleasure they have taken in unrighteousness. "That all mny be judged who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness." It follows: (a) That error is not an innocent thing, It has practical issues of the most momentous character. (b) That it is a frart'ul perversion of the human soul to take pleasure in what God hates. (c) That God allows the sin and madness of men to develop themselves to their fullest extent. (d) That God in thi~ 32 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS. [oe. 11. 1-17.

way will be finally justified in their judgment; he "will be justified in his speaking, "nd shall be clear in bis jndging" (Ps, li. 4).-T. C.

VeI'II. 13, 14.-Apostolic thanh;giving for the election and lhe calling of the Thessa- lonians. I. Tm; DrVINE ELECTION. "God bath from tlu beginning chosen you." 1. There is an "elecr ion acco,·ding to grace" (Rom. xi. 6). lt is not to be confounded with the calling, which is an effect of it. " Whom he predestinated, them he also called" (Rom. viii. 30). Our salvation is always traced to "his own purpose and grace which was given us in Christ Je_sus before the world beg-an." 2. Tl,e date of the election, "From the beginning." It is "from the foundation of tho world" (Eph. i. 4) and therefore does not rest upon the personal claims of individuals. 3. The means ~f the election. "In sanctification or the Spirit and belief of the truth." The election is to the means as well as the end; it cannot take effect without the means. There is an objective as well a.s a subjective side in the sphere of the election. (1) The sanctifica- tion of the Spirit. This is the objective side. (a) It implies a spiritual change of nature. The Spirit applies the salvation, and regeneration is his first work. (b) Sancti- fication is the evidence as well as the fruit of election. (2) " The belief of the truth." This is the subjective side. Man is not passive in his salvation. (a) As the Spirit is the agent, the truth is the instrumeut of salvation. (b) The truth must be believed in order to salvation. As men are chosen to be saints, they are chosen also to be believers. (3) The necessary connection between the sanctification and the belief. It might appear as if the belief of the truth ought to precede the sanctification of the Spirit. But there cannot he faith without the operation of the Spirit, while, on the other hand, the sanctification 1s "through the truth." The two are inseparably joined together. 4. The end of the ekcticm. "God bath chosen you to salvation." (1) It is not an election to Church privileges. (2) Nor to national privileges. (3) But to salvation itself. (a) This is salvation from sin and sorrow, death and hell. (b) It is" the end of our faith" (1 Pet. i. 9). II. THE DIVINE CALLING. "Wbercunto he called you by our gospel, to the obtaining of the glory of our Lor<l Jesus Christ." The election issues in the call. 1. The AU,thor of the call. God. "Th,-re is one Lawgiver who is able to save and to destroy." He has the right to ca.11 aud the power to call. Nothing but Divine power can save the soul 2. The means of the call. "Our gospel.n The ministry of the Word was the great instrument in the Spirit's hand of their conversion. 3. The end of the call. (1) It was to obtain the )!lory of Christ. It was to be obtained, not purchased or wrought out by their personal righteousness. (2) Believers are to share in the very glory of their Redeemer.-T. C.

entries.title: 2TH 2:15
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content:
-E:chortation to a steadfast maintenance of apostolic traditions, "Therefore stand fast, &nd hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or oar Epistle." L 'l'HE GROUND OF TBJS EXHORTATION. It was their election and calling. There is a perfect consistency between the Divine election and the obligations of Christian duty, II. THE NECESSITY oF CHRISTIAN STABU.ITY. It was specially needful at Thessalo- nica, in the midst of the agitations and ehakings and restlessness that prevailed on the snbject of the secoud advent. down from some one anterior to the apostle, and from the apostle banded down to the Thessalonians; nor were they committed to the Tbessaloniane to be banded down to future ages. 'J'here is an entire equality between them, seeing the blessing: is attributed to both. 8. There i, oneness of essence, as is indicated by the singular verb used in the passage. II. THE GROUND OF EXPECTATION THAT THE BLESSINGS ASKED WILL BB GIVEN. "Who loved us, and gave us everlasting consolation and good hope through grace." l. The Divine love is the true ground of all our hopes of blessing, for it is everlasting, unchangeable, practical in its ends. 2. The two elements in the Divine gift. (1) "Everlasting consolation." (a) A source of unfailing comfort in the midst of the trials of life, springing out of everlasting sources and sufficing to all eternity; for God is a "God of all comfort," and " if there be any consolation," it is in Christ. (b) This comfort is a gift-a mark of Divine favour, not of human merit. (2) "A good hope through grace." (a) This is "the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before the world began" (Titus i. 2). (b) It is a good hope (11) because of its Author; (13) because of its foundation, "through grace;" (-y) because of its purifying effects (l John iii. 4). Ill THE BLEssrnas PRAYED FOB. 1. "Thou hast put gladness into my heart." 2. Establishment and pe1·severance. "And stablish you in every good word and work." (1) This blessing is to be sought especially in restless and unset tied times. (~) Stability is to be sought in" every good word," so that believers may not be carried away by "winds of doctrine;" and in "every good work," so that they may not be shaken by doubt and thus become restless and disorderly in conduct. entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content:
-The day of (!hriat not immediate. I. THE MISTAXE OF THE THESSALo- NIANS. 1. In itself. The day of the Lord is present; it is already dawning; it is close upon us. 'l'his thought had taken possession of their souls; it filled their hearts; it left no room for ordinary commonplace duties. They were neglecting these in their strong excitement, in their eager anticipation of the approach of the great day. What was the use of attention to business, of daily labour, of the quiet r,erfurmance of their accustomed tasks, when the Lord was to be expected at once, when they were to be caught up, away from earth and its employments, to meet the Lord in the air. "We which are alive and remain shall be caught up," St. Paul bad said in his First Epistle. They misunderstood his words; they supposed that it must be during their own lifetime; that it might be, that it would be, immediate. 2. Its origin. Spirit, word, or letter. "Believe not every spirit" (St. John said); "try the spirits whether they are :f God." There were utterances which claimed to be inspired and were not so. The discerning of spirits was one of the manifold gifts of the Holy Ghost. It was their duty not to despise prophesying, but yet to prove all things. 'l'liere were also words quoted as if spoken by St. Paul ; letters, too, purporting to come from him. Men misrepresented him; they attributed the sayings of others, their own, perhaps, to the holy apostle; even letters, it seems, ware current, said to be th_e apostle's, but ~ot really his. People are perplexed often nowadays by the many differences of opinion which exist among Ohristians. The fact of this uiversity is to some an excuse for unbelief or for sloth in spiritual things; to others, a real temptation, a great trial of faith. But we see it has been so from the beginning. There were err.. rs of belief ~n this infant Church of 'l'hessalonioa while th@ apostle, who had founded lt, was still II, THEBSALONIANS. D 34 THE SECOND EPISTLE '1'0 THE THESSALONIANS. near at band-at Coiintb. Even in th8l'8 early days things which he had said were misunderstood; his authority was claimed for words which he had never spoken , and strangest of all, there were written letters bearing his name which were falsely as~ribed t.o him. We ba1·e our trials now. We are troubled, some of us, by the difficulties which arise from various readings or interpretations, by the doubts thrown by modern writers on this or that book of Holy Scripture, by the conflict of opinions in the Church. It is some comfort to think ~hat we of this ~ge are not alone in our temptations; our position is not one of such smgular perplexity as some of us are apt to think. If we persevere in prayer, if we try to live by faith looking to the Lord Jesus Christ the doubts which vex us will soon be clean•d away. ' II. ST. PAUL'S WAY OF DEALING WITH THAT MISTAKE. 1. He beseeches them. He i1 very gen tie with his convert■, very earnest too, and affectionate; full of'deep anxiety for their spiritual welfare. Aud it was a matter of great importance. St. Paul had dwelt much upon the coming of the Lord. The Parousiawas a subject of much excited talk, much stirring of heart among the Thessalonians. St. Paul had spoken in his First Epistle of" our gathering together unto him;" how •• we that are alive and remain shall be caught up in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air." It was a prospect very blessed, 1·ery awful too; it had been opened out in strong, startling words. They inferred from his way of expressing himself that it was very close at hand, to be looked for immediately ; their excitement was intense. He beseeches them to listen. 2. They must be calm. Religion lies in e. calm, quiet walk with God. It has its emotions, they are at times deep and strong; it bas its enthusiasm, bnt it is ordered and grave. They must not allow themselves to be shaken from their settledjudgment; they must not give way to this trembling, uneasy excitement. They must return to the quiet, steady discharge of the common duties of life; their best strength was in quietness und confidence. This was the best preparation for the ooming of Christ. '!'hat coming waa not immediate; much was to happen first. LES&ONS. 1. Learn to be sober, thoughtful, to distrust excitement, to live in patient continuance of well-doing. 2. There will be difficulties, perplexitieil; they are trials of faith; they must be endured in patience and overcome by faith. 3. Prepare for the coming of Christ. The best prepe.re.tion is to perform each duty e.s it comes in faith and prayer e.s Ullto the Lord.-B. C. C.
