entries.title: 2TH 2:3–12
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content:
-Tlie man of Bin. I. HE MUST OOME BEFORE THE DAY OF TBE LORD. 1. Hi.s revel,ation. He is antichrist-the evil counterpart of the most holy Saviour; he has his revelation, his apocalypse. There must be e.n apostasy before the coming of the Lord-a great, notable apostasy. The apostle bad warned the 'l'hessalonians of it; we need these warnings now. We must not be discouraged when we see scepticism, unbelief, rampant around us. These things must be; Holy Scripture has forewarned us. We must be prepared; we must be calm and steadfast, looking for the coming of the Lord. Such apostasies there have been ; there have been precursors of the man of sin, such e.s Caligula shortly before the date of this Epistle, or Nero shortly after. There have been evil men among the popes of Rome who have exhibited in their lives some of tLe characteristic features of the antichrist. But the apostasy is yet to come; the man of sin is yet in the future; the mystery of iniquity is working even now; it is working below the surface, in secret; hereafter, we know not when, it will burst forth into open day in the revelation of the man of sin. We mnst not look forward to a continual, unopposed progress of the gospel ; we must not expect that religion will go on in everextended triumphs, with no checks, no defeats, overspreading the earth more and more with itl! blessed influences. Such an expectation is not warranted either by Scripture or by the sig1,s of the times. Scripture tells us of the coming apostasy, of the revelation of the man of sin. And in the world the forces of unbelief and evil are evidently gathering themselves for a mighty conflict. In our own country, it is true, there has been a great revival of religious zeal, great love for Christ, much earnest, self-denying work for his sake. But alon~side of this there has been a great outburst of infidelity, a widespread scepticism, e. hatred of revelation, manifesting itself in the life and works of men of learning and culture; while elsewhere the revolt age.inst all forms of authority, Divine and human, h11B been more outapoken and far more widely spread. The armies uf God and Satan, tJ.~ powers of good and evil, light and de.rkoeae, faith and unbelief, oe. lL 1-17.] 'l'HE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE Tm:SSALONIANS. 36

seem to be already marshalled In preparation for an awful struggle. It must come Holy Script11re warns us; it will culminate in the revelation of the man of sin. H~ will be revealed-out of previous obscurity; the apparition will be unveiled out of darkness. 2. His character. He is a ptrson, a man of miahty intellect and 11iant strenatb of will, who will tuke advantage of a general develop~ent of unbelief and la.wlessn;88 and gain for a time a widespread sovereignty. Sin fills his being; it becomes, as ii were, incarnate in him; it domi11ates his entire personality. He is "a son of perdition• like Judas (compare the common Hebraism, "a son of death"), destined himseli' to eternal death, involving in utter death all who follow him. He is an adversary, a. human Sa.tan, filled with all the awful energy, the concentrated malice of the evil one. He is the antichrist, the avowed and bitter enemy of the holy Saviour, bringing with his intense wickedness the horrible cry of" Ecrasez l'infame I" into awful prominence. He exalts himself against every one that is called God; he sits in the temple of God, reviving the madness of Antiochus Epiphanes, the impious attempt of Caligula.. Such a. man the world has not yet seen. There have been many outbursts of wickedness, many evil men in the long course of history have risen to sovereign power; but no one yet has combined in himself a.II the characteristics ascribed to the man of sin in this Epistle. It is a. fearful spectacle which is yet to come. St. Paul warned the Thessalonians that such things there would be, uprisings of malice and persecution, anticipations of the wan of sin. He warns the whole Church throughout all time that such things a.re to be looked for; that sooner or later, before the end cometh, the man of sin himself shall be revealed in all the awful energy of unmingled wickedness, relieved by no one trace of goodness. II. THE OBSTACLE. 1. The Thessalonian& knet0 what it waa. St. Paul had told them of this during his short residence in Thcssalonica. For some reason he had dwelt much on this awl11l subject; it must have been necessary for the Thessalonia.ns in their special circumstances, though we know not why. They had knowledge which we have not; they knew precisely what we cannot find out for certain with all our searching. We may be satisfied that this knowledge, then good for them, is not now necessary for us, or it would have been more clearly reveale<l. "Ye have an unction from the Holy One," St. John says of believers, "and ye know all things"-all that we need to know for life and godliness. 2. What was it 1 The Roman empire, the power of Roman law, the emperor as embodying that power. This was the answer of most ancient writers; it seems to be the most common answer now. Then the power of Rome checked the outuurst of anarchy and lawlessness. It is still tbe majesty of law, the authority of well-ordered governments, that fulfils the same office. The mystery of lawlessness is working now; it has not reached its height, it has not embodied itself in the fearful personality of the man of sin. But it is working; and it is a mystery, the terrible counterpart of the mystery of godliness. There is a mystery in evil, a strange, fearful mystery, dark secrets not yet revealed; a. mystery which suggests awful, heart-rending questionings-questionings which can be quieted only in his presence who giveth rest to the troubled, anxious soul. This mystery of lawlessness was working even then in the world which the God of love created; it is working now; but it is held down by the restraining power; it cannot give birth to the man of sin till his time shall come, the time foreordained in the counsels of God. Then the restraining power will be taken out of the way; lawlessness will prevail, and its creature and embodiment, the lawless one, will come. III. HIS AOTIVITY. 1. It is but/or a shr:Yrt time. 'l'he Lord Jesus shall destroy him, and that in an instant, when he cometh. He needs only to speak the word of power; the breath of his mouth shall sweep the adversary into that perditiou to which be was appointed. 'l'he manifestation of his coming, the very sight of the awful Judge, shall slay the wicked one. This must be our consulatiou whon the dark problems of life distress our souls-" the Lord cometh." 'l'hen shall come the assured triumph of righteousness, the crowning victory over all the powe~s of evil 2. Bu~ it is treme:nd~. As God is revealed in Christ, so is Sa.tan revealed m the man of sm, the a.nt.ichnst. Tho "miracles and wonders and signs" (Aots ii. 22) which God di<l by Obrist a.re parodied by the power and _sigus and w".nde~ which Sat~n w~ll w~rk through the age~cy of the ma.u of sin. As.Chnst's coming 1s with power, with his mtghty angels 1n fla.mrng fire, so is the coming of the lawless one with all power according to the working of 38 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS. [cu. 11. 1-1~

Satan. AB Goo work<>th in his sRints both to l\•ill and to do of his good p\e11sure, so Satan worketh in this his representative with Ali the awful energy of diabolical wioked- .:iess. The antichrist, SD.ys llengel, stands in !he same relation to Satan as Christ to llod. The anticliri~t will work miracles, but they are by the energy of Satan wond,.rs l)f falsehond. They are not mere deceptions, they are real miracles; but they are the works of h,m who is the father of lies; and they are lies, inasmuch as they aro intcn,led to mislead m<'n into worshipping him as God who is the personation or t-atan, the liar from tlie beginning. Lies, too, they are, because they are the signs of a power which is only a miserable impost11re, which must soon end in death and ruin. Our Lord has warned us (Matt. xxiv. 24) of false Christs and false prophets whose signs and wonders should be so startling as to deceive, if it were possible, the very elect. The false prophet, the second beast, of the RevelRtion doeth great wonders, so that he maketh fire to come down from heaven, and deceiveth them that dwell ou the earth by the means of those miracles which he bath power to do. Then there may be, there will be false miracles, l~·ing wonders. Miracles alone do not always prove the ag;ency of God: but miracles with holiness, works of faith issuing out of a life filled with the presence of God. The blessed life of Jesus Christ our Lord is a mightier miracle than the physical wonders which he wrom:ht. A life of perfect purity and transcendent holiness in the weakness ofhumau flesh, amid all the temptations of this wicked world, is to us a more condncin;.:: proof of the Divine mission of Christ than the signs from heaven would have been which the Jews so often asked for. The Church must expect the coming of lying wondC'rs; she must stand unshaken amid all the developments of t-atanic energy. The elect will not be deceivecl, for they will recognize the notes of antichrist, "all the deceivableness of unrighteousness;" they will remember the warn- ings of lloly Scripture: "Whosoever doeth not righteousness is not of God," "He that committeth sin is of the devil; for the devil sin11eth from the beginning." IV. ITS RESULT. 1. He deceiveth them that dwell on the earth; not the elect--the souls of the righteous are in the ha11d of God; but those who have not been sealed with that Holy Spirit of promise which is the earnest of our inheritance, the pledge of that seal of the living God which his angel shall one day set upon the foreheads of his chosen. But there are, alas! those that are perishing, who have not passed from death unto life through faith in the Son of God, but still abide in death. Such men the man of sin, the lawless one, deceives and engulfs in his own utter destruction. 2. Their own wuful11ess is the cause of their ruin. "God is not willing that any should perish." The true light lighteth every man. It came to them, but they received it not. They received not Christ. He is the Truth, and he is Love. He came into the world that the world through him might be saved. But they received not him who is the Way, the Truth, and the Life. They had no love for the truth, no desire for it. They were quite indifferent to the truth, though their conscience told them that it was the truth; they were worse than indifferent, they rejected it. They might have been saved; the truth would have made them free. They mi~ht have been sa11ctified through the truth; for the tru1b of God, receive,! into the heart, hath power to cleanse, to purify, to save the soul. Il11L they loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil. 3. It end.a in judicial bli11dne&1J. God's Spirit will not always strive with man. In his awful justice he gives over to a reprobate mind those who per8cvere in disobedience. He sendeth them a strong delusion, a working of error. As virtue is its own reward, so sin ii its own puni8hmcnt. Eternal sin (see Mark iii. 29 in the best-supported reading) is the fearful end of the obstinate sinner. That hardening of the heart, in which l,abitual sin must at last re8ult, is ascribed in Huly Scriplure sometime~ to God, 1ome• times to the sinner himself, ~ometime~ to the dcccitfuluesH of sin. '!'hey are different modes of expressing the 1111me law of God'11 gover11ment. He has so ordered our moral nature, that sin, when it is full grown, briugeth forth death. He lets the rebel have his own will; he leaves him to be "lord of himself, that heritage of woe." The Spirit is witl1<!rnwn at last from those who vex, grieve, resist, his gracious influences. But there id something more awful still. Not only did the Spirit of the Lor,1 depart from Sau!, but" en evil ~pirit from the Lorrl troublerl him." God himself sends at the last, in his most a"·ful j,,6tice, the strung delusion, tho inworking of error. It is the lasl state, worse 1J,a11 tlie first; after which comes thnt rlreadful sentence, "It is Impossible . • • io renew til!'m again unto repentance." 'l'his thought gh·es a most terrible on. 11. 1-17.] THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANB. 17

significance to every act of wilful, unrepented ein; e'Yery such act brings a man nearer (how near he cennot tell) to that most awful state whence there is no repenta11ce. Then comes judicial blindness; the light that was within them becomes darkness. 'l'h_ey would not believe the truth of God, now they believe the lie of the man of oin. It 1s the judgment of God. We see indications of it from time to time in the credulity of unbelief, Men who reject the Bible are sometime3 ready to believe anything except the Bible; they will greedily accept any legend, any scientific hypothesis, though evidently not more than a provisional hypotheRis, which seems to contradict the Bible; they will deify hurnauity, they will worship the idol which is the creature of their own thoughts rather than the living God, This unbelief sprang out of sin; they "had pleasure in unrighteousness." '!'here is such a thing as honest doubt; such were the doubts of Asaph, of Thomas. But unbelief in a very large measure comes from moral causes. Sin darkens the heart and the mind; sin always leads to practical, often to intellectual, unbelief. "Every one that doeth evil hateth the light;" he walketb in darkness; he seeth not the coming judgment. LESSONS, 1. Be prepared for times of darkness-they must come; be strong in faith. 2. If unbelief becomes dominant, still believe; God has forewarned us. 3. An~rchy, confusion, leads to the predominance of sin. "Give peace in our time, 0 Lord." 4. Even miracles may deceive. Christ rcmaineth faithful; trust always in him. 5. Hate sin with utter hatred ; it ends in harciness of heart.-B. C. C.

entries.title: 2TH 2:13–17
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content:
-St. Paul's hopes /qr the Thessaloniana. L HE THANKS Gon FOB BIB PAST lllEROIES SHOWN TO THEM. 1. For their election. He tnrns from prophecies of coming terrors to thoughts ol hope and consolation. He repeats the vror<ls of eh. i. 3, "Weare bound to give thanks." He felt the greatness of God's mercies to the Thessalonians. Mercies ~hown to them were shown to him; he so dearly loved them. It was his bounden duty to thank God for them; how much more was it their c!.!:ty to be thankful for the grace grauted to th,·m I God had set his love upon them; God had chosen them from the beginning. This was the source of their blessedness; not any merits, any good deeds, of theirs. All our hopes rest on the electing grace of God. That thought is full of sweet, pleasant, and unspeakable comfort to godly persons. It was II,) to the Thessalonian Christians, especially at this time, when awful anticipations of the coming end were casting a dark shadow over them. That election manifests itself in holiness of life. The seal of the Spirit is the earnest, the pledge, of the heavenly inheritance. God's elect must feel within themselves the working of the Spirit of Christ, mortil'ying the works of the flesh, and their earthly members, and drawing up their minds to high and heavenly things. The sanctification of the Spirit is the sphere in which the life of election moves and energizes. And with the growth of holiness in the heart faith is ever deepened and strengthened. The working of the Spirit greatly confirms the faith of eternal sal, vation to be enjoyed through Christ; it convinces the Christian soul with a might:, power, with the certainty of intuition, of the reality of the great truths of the gospel, so that the Christian walks in ever-increasing faith, in the power of that victory which overcometh the world. 2. For the hope of glory. God had predestinated the 'l'hessalonians to be conformed to the image of his Son; by the preaching of St. Paul he had called them to that state of salvation. They were living in a present salvation; they were looking forwards to a future glory ; their high hope was the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. His glory will be the glory of his saints, for he has given it then; (John xvii. 22). 'l'hey are heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ. All that Christ has is theirs in hope; for Christ himself is theirs, and they arc Christ's. The Christian who cherishes this high and blessed hope must live in couti11ual thankfulness. II. HE URGES 'l'HEIII TO STEADFASTNESS. L Jn the life ,:f faith. Stand fast, he says; fight the good fight of faith. You must do your part. God has chosen you; he has given you his Spirit; he has called you to salvation. Yet,fOU must work out that salva- tion. We need not perplex ourselves with the deep mysteries which thought cannot fathom; in practice, the duty of perseverance follows from the electing grace of God. He has chosen yon; persevere, for he gives you the power; be steadfast, for }'OU owe 11 great debt of g, atitude to him who has so greatly loved you. 2. In doctrine. Uold the traditions. St. Paul had taught the 'l'hessalonians by word of mouth. We must remember that in all probability not one of our four Gospels was vet written. The 38 rHE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE Tm:SSALONIANS. [oa. u. 1-17

TbeBSRloniRns knew the history of our Lord's life and death, and the doctrines of the Christian faith, only through the ornl teaching of St. Paul, The First Epistle was the only part of the New Testament Scriptures known to them; probably the only part as yet in existence. St. Paul had taught orally for several years before he began to write. Oral teaching was oftm misunderstood, often forgotten, as this Epistle shows. Uut the teach- Ing of an apostle, whether by word or by writing, was a precious deposit, for that which he deli\"ered to his converts he had himself received of the Lord. Be it ours to continue steadfast in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship. m. HE su11s UP ms HOPES IN A BENEDICTION. 1. He points eliem to God. The clause begins in the Greek with the emphatic 11b,-lls, himself. ,ve must stand fast, we must persevere ; but it is he who establishes the hearts of his chosen; he only is our everlasting Strength, the Rock of ages. The apostle in this place, as in 2 Cor. xiii. 14, puts the Sadour's name first, because it is by Christ that we have access to the Father. We feel that this order would have been incongruous, impossible, unless Christ were i11deed God; we feel that the singular verb could not be used, as it is twice, in ver. 17, unless he and the Father were one (comp. 1 Thess. iii. 11). God the Father is our F!!ther, St. Paul says emphatically. He loved us; on his fatherly love rests our election, our hope of !!lory. He has given already to his saints eternal comfort, a comfort independent of the changes and chances of this earthly life-a comfort eternal, for it rests on him who is eternal; and with that comfort which is present, though not temporal, not confined within the limits of time, he has given also 11, good hope of future glory, the blessed hope of everlasting life with God in heaven. And this he has given in grace, in the encompassing atmosphere of his favour, without merit or works of ours. 2. He prays that God's blessing may still rest upon them. He who loved them, and gave them eternal comfort and good hope, will surely comfort and establish them, His first gifts are a pledge of their continuance. He will not leave his work unfinished. His love is like himself, eternal He can sheJ that blessed comfort into the heart, the inmost seat of joy and sorrow. ,vhen there is hidden comfort there, outward troubles may cause sorrow, but cannot take away the fuluess of joy. He can establish our heart; he can give us that established heart, fixed, trusting in the Lord (Ps. cxii. 7, 8), which the world, the flesh, the devil, cannot shake. Then we shall speak only words of truth and love, and do only works of righteousness and faith through that inner comfort and strength which comes from God alone. LEssoNs. 1. In the midst of dangers there is comfort for the saints ; they are in the hands of God; God hath chosen them. 2. Look for the evidence of God's election in holiness of life ; without holiness we cannot see him. 3. Be steadfast; make your calling and election sure; take heed lest ye fall. 4. Only God can give "eternal comfort." Seek that precious gift of him ; it is given to those whom he stablishes in every good word and work.-B. C. C.

entries.title: 2TH 2:1–12
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content:
-.Antichrilt. L ErutoB BEGABDING THE COMING OF CHRIST. "Now we beseech you, brethren, touching the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and our gathering together unto him; to the end that ye be not quickly shaken from your mind, nor _,·et be troubled. either by spirit, or by word, or by Epistle as from us, as that tl,e Jay of the Lord is now present; let no man beguile you in any wise." The apostle beseeches the 'l'h,-ssalonians as brethren, in the interest of correct views of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is his principal topic in both Epistles. The comfurting side of the coming is the gathering together of all believers unto him, never to be followed by a separation, as set forth in I 'l'hess. iv. 17, "'Then we that are alive, that arc left, shall together with them" (the d,ad in Christ who bav& been raised)" be caught up in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord." By the way in which he introduces this gathering together, it can be seen that i., was very attractive to him. It was that in the corning which he especially wished to be conserved. In the beginning of 1 These. v. the apostle had distinctly taught the uncertainty of the time of the coming. But representations bad been made to the Tb-lonians that the day of the Lord was actually beginning. 'l'hree form• which these representations might take, or, more probably, did take, arespecifted. '!'here were representation, founded upon pretended prophecy. There were also representationa fowtded upon an alleged oral communication of the apostle. There were further repre- on. u. 1-17.J 'l'HE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS. 3~

sente.tions founded upon an alleged Epistle of the apostle. The existence and circuiation of e. fabricated Epistle seem to be hinted at in the words at the close of this Epistle: "The salutation of me Paul with mine own han<l, which is the token in every Epistle: so I write." If the Thesse.lonians accepted of these representations, there was danaer of their being precipire.tely shaken from their composure of mind and even thrown° into a terrified state, e.s at sea men e.re discomposed and even horrified by the bursting of e. storm upon them. The apostle, therefore, considered it necessary to write this Epistle to put them on their guard against their being led away by these representations. Let no me.n beguile them in these we.ye, or, making it wider, in e.ny other way. II. 'l'HE ANTICHRISTUN MANIFESTATION. 1. The ccming of (Jhrist to b, preced«I by apostasy. "For it will not be, except the falling away come first." "Aposta..sy" (aft.er the Greek) is the more technical word-the apost~sy of which the Thessalonian& had been t.old. There is, particularly, meant falling away from the faith of Christ. It ii a movement begun by those who have been within the Christian circle, and who, after having been advantaged by Christianity in outward enlightenment and quickening, have ungratefully turned away. Or the movement away from Christ may dishonourably be encoura~ed by those who still remain witliin the Christian circle, but have lost faith in the distinctive teachings of Christianity. The name of" apostate" has been given to the Empc-ror Julian for his signal renunciation of Christianity, but it is a name which belongs to every one who in the struggle of life parts with his early Christian convictions, his good traditions. Let us see that we are not, in the smallest degree, contributing to the mov~ ment away from Christ. 2. The revelation of the man of ,in, " And the man of sin be reveaied." It is now an exploded idea that the man of sin means popery. The principal interpreters-Olshausen, Ellicott, Alford, Eadie-bold to the idea of the man of sin being a person. He is supposed to be the last and worst product of the apostasy. He is a caricature of Christ, having a mystery, and revelation, and miracles, and claim of divinity, a coming and preparation, even as Christ has. He is a.s inclusive of all the bad forms of humanity, as Christ is of all itR good forms. It cannot be said of this most unlovely conception that it has the similitude of truth. It cannot be dogmatically laid down as a matter of interµretation that the man ol sin is a person, any more than the restrainer is a person. The designation" man of sin" points, in the first place, to sin as the essence of the apostasy. The moving away from Christ is an opposing of the Divine authority. The designation "man of sin" points, in the second place, to sin as working under human (not angelic) conditions, and, taken along with apostasy, point:! especially to the development of sin in human history. The designation "man of sin"points, in the third place, t-0 this historical development, not as actual, but as idealized. As the language, "0 man of God," is a call to consider the true ideal of manhood, so the man of sin may be viewed as the ideal of the development of sin among men. In so far as popery is after this ideal may it be said to be the man of sin. In so far a.s any of us take after the bad ideal of manhood may it be said to us, " 0 man of sin !" calling us to consider what we are following after. Let us see that we do not in the least merit the designation. By the revelation of the man of sin is to be understood the bringing out of the real nature of sin. It may put on specious forms, but it is essential vile- ness; it is uglier than the ugliest of creatures, it is more venomous than the serpent, it is more grovelling than the earth-worm, it is blocker than darkness. And in the working of Providence in human history, it is intended that this should be, with accumulating evidence and unmistakably, brought out. And we are here taught that there cannot be the revelation of Christ at his coming until all that is evil in sin has been brought out. 3. The son of perdition. "The son of perdition." The common Hebrew form is followed. Sprung from perdition, he bas perdition as his destiny. The designation marks the result of the movement away from Christ. Every such movement must prove in the end abortive. How many of those movements that once had vitality in them have already ended in perdition I The designation was given by our Lord to Judas Iscariot : "An,1 none of them is lost, but the son of perdition." And it is certainly not to be wondered at that he whose apostasy was aggravated by the proximity in which he stood to Christ should strikingly be shown in his suicidal end to be the son of perdition. In so fe.r as any of us are moving away from Christ we are placing our paternity iu perdition, and are working out perdition as our ,lestiny. Let us, then, be 1,\/arned by what will yet be S!len to come out of sin. 4. The opposer of Ch-r-i,t. "He that 40 THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS. [oH, 11, 1-17,

oppo!ll!th." It ie not said, "He that opposeth Uhrist," but, from the way in which Christian thought is interwoven with the whole paragraph, we may understand that to be the meKning. We may, therefore, regard the movement as described by the designation "antichrist" with which John supplies us. As it is in its origin a movement away from Christ, so it comes to have the character of being directed against Christ. It is a moveml'nt in which advantage~ gained from Christ are unworthily used against him. As it is ~h~ object ~f God in ~he _Church to put forward Christ f?r the acceptance of men, so 1t 1s the ob3cct of ant1chnst to draw away men from Chnst; Popery is anti- christ in so far as it does not give Christ and his words and his death their proper plaee in Christian belief and life. It may be said of 118 that we are antichrist in so far as we do not yield ourselves up to Christ, and do not to our utmost ability help forward the cause of Christ. "He that is not with me is against me, and he that gathereth not with me scattercth abroad." 5. The deifi,er 'JI srif. "And exalteth himself a<>ainst all that is called God or that is worshipped; so that he sitteth in the temple of God setting himself forth as God." There is strong confirmation here of the doctrine of Muller, that all sin is of the nature of selfishness. Antichrist is selfishness rising to the impious height of self-deification. He raises himself above and against him who is truly called God, without thereby falling into idolatry; for he also raises himself above and against those that have only the name of gods, and, it is added (going beyond the actually named), above and against all that can be turned into an object of worship. He noes not, therefore, shut out the sacred sphere ; rather does he fill it with himself. He is the centre of all 1visdom, power, and glory for which worship is due. The startlin" language is that be sitteth in the temple of God, setting himself forth as God. Ther~ is supposed to be meant a Ression in the actual temple in Jerusalem by those who, laying undue stress upon the langnage here, regard the paragraph as having already received its fulfilment. But there is reference to the actual temple only by way of illustra- tion. As God was represented as sitting between the cherubim, requiring the adoration of all Israelites (as be was the object of adoration to the highest intelligences), so antichrist entertains the thon!!ht of divinity and strictly requires adoration. While in Christ's consciousness of divinity there was the element of infinite self-sacrifice, in antichrist's presumptuous thought of divinity there is only the element of utter selfishness. We are not to think here merely of him who sits in the Church and arrogantly wields spiritual power. Rather are we to see the tendency of the whole movement away from Christ. This is how it aims at expressing itself. This is the dreadful interpretation of what it would be at. And it is true of us all, in so far as we are selfish, that we are aiming at making a temple for ourselves in which to sit down and to require adoration. AI. we in our present state of feeling can only recoil from such self-deification, let us beware of that selfishness which is at the heart of sin. 6. The T/,essalonians reminded offormer teachings on the above points. "Remember ye not, that, when I was yet with you, I told you these things?" 1n his teachings on the coming he was not corrected or supplemented by recent revelation. He had occupied the same position from the beginning; such is undoubtedly his own contention, and is against the contention of some who attribute to him that he believed that he would live to see the coming. He reminds the 'l'hessalonians here, not without some measure of blame, that when he was with them (and he singles out himself in making this statement) he told them some things which he was now putting down in his letter. III. THE BESTBAINING POWER. 1. What restrains the antichristian manifestati()'II,. • And now ye know that which restraineth, to the end that he may be revealed in his own seasoa." This was another point on which he had given them information. It is left indefinite what the restraining power is. 'l'he prevailing opinion, as expressed by Ellicott, is "u·ell-ordered hu:rr,an rule, the principles of l~gality as opposed to those of lawlessness~{ which the Roman empire was the then embodiment and manifestation." It is true that civil rule keeps back many of the manifestations of evil. The ci vii ruler is a terror to evil-doers. If men were allowed to give vent to their evil passions without drt-ad of punishment, this world would be a pandemonium. But, at the same time, it is true that the worst manifestations of evil, of proud defiance of God, of bitter rancour against Christ (which are chiefly to be thought of in connection with the anticbristio:n movement), are those with which the civil magistrate has little to do, The condition upon which these manifestations depend is rather the increased setting forth oH. 11. 1-17.J THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS. 41

of _Christ, There is a manifestation of good going forward, as well as a manifestation of evil. It must yet be shown in human history that there is an essential loveliness belonging to tho Christian life. Many Scriptures promise a period of conquest for the Church. ·when the Church extends its conquests there will be a solidarity of i11fluence on the side of Christ of which no adequate conception can now be formed. The result of that wi)l be, om_ong those who participate in the antichristian movement, deepened hat~ed ag!lmst Christ. As when he conquered on the cross there was a calling forth agamst him of the worst elements especially of superhuman evil, so when he advances to conquest in human history there will be a similar calling forth of the worst elements especially of human evil. The time when evil is thus powerfully to be revealed has been fixed by God. It may be said that the apostle should, according to the inter- pretation, have regarded the Christian manifestation as coming to a head. But it was open to him to regard it under a special aspect as that which in its yet partial character held back the full manifestation of antichrist. 2. The present working of the mystery of lawlessness. "For the mystery of lawlessness doth already work." "Lawlessness," which corresponds to "sin," formerly used, is not to be taken as fe.vourin,( the view that the restraining power is human rule. It points to the antichristian movement as characterized by a disposition to cast off all authority, especially the highest authority. 'l'he stress is to be laid on" mystery." Evil was then working, and in working was revealing itself, but its true nature as opposition to Christ was largely concealed, was only very partially revealed. A lurid light was thrown npon it by the ten great persecutions which, under the Roman emperors, were directed against Christianity. Light is thrown upon it by the attacks which in the present day are made upon Christianity. But it would seem that we have not seen all that is in it of opposition to Christ. The mystery of lawlessness still works. 3. The removal of the restrainer. "Only there is one that restraineth now, until he be taken ont of the way. And then shall be revealed the lawless one, whom the Lord Jesus shall slay with the breath of his mouth, and bring to nought by the manifestation of his coming." Ellicott regards the use of the masculine gender as a realistic touch, by which what was previously expressed by the more abstract "restraining power" is now represented as concrete and personified. It is strange how this should not be regarded as applying also to the "lawless one" to whom the restrainer is here opposed. If the restrainer is human rule, then his removal must mean the upturning (apparently general) of human rule. And that is what is contemplated by some as the conclusion to human history. But the restrainer being "Christianity not come to the season of its full manifestation," his removal must mee.n the arrival of that season. When Christianity, working among the multitudes of men, brings its full influence to bear on the antichristian movement, in what it calls forth of opposition, that movement will come to the completeness of it8 exposure. And antichrist, thus morally defeated, eternally disproved, will h:ive taken away from it its sphere of operation. It will be slain with the breath of Christ's mouth, and brought to nought by the manifestation of his coming. IV. THE LYING CHARACTER OF THE ANTIOHRISTIAN MOVEMENT. 1. Liea of Satan. "Even he, whose coming is according to the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders." As Satan is a liar and the father of lies, so the antichristian movement which he inspires is characterized by lying. As Christ has power and signs and wonders of truth, so the antichristian movement bas power and signs and wonders of lying. It is remarkable that the Church of Rome puts forward a claim of miracle-working, which helps it to preserve its influence over miu,ls, bnt which it cannot establish. The power and signs and wonders by which men are apt to bJ deluded now are mure of an intellectual nature. It is objected to Christianity that the mirades . with which it is bound up are shown by science to be impossible. lt is objected that it presents too severe a \'iew of our human condition, in representing us as standing in need of salvation. It is objected thnt it presents too severe a view of the character of God, in representing him as punishing sin in Christ. It is objected that it presents too severe a view of human duty, in calling upon us to for~ake all and follow Christ. When these objections are powerfully presented, and so as to have the appearance of s:iving the character of God from e.spersions, there may be the effect, which false miracles have often had, of men being deluded. 2. Lies of Satan leading to unr,:,,ldeo- ness. "With all deceit of unrighteousness." When men entertain false views, 42 THE SECOND EPISTLE 'l'O THE THESSALONIANS. [on. n. 1-17,

espeoially of the oh&racter of God, there is &n e&sy transitio!l to unriahteousness. There are many ways in which they can persuade themselves, that they ~ay exercise liberty in their manner of living. They do not need to pray to God ; they do not need to rend God's Book ; they do not need to keep God's day ; they do not need to be strictly honourable in their transactions; they do not need to make sacrifices for others. It is enough that they keep up an appearance of probity and purity, and it may be of religion( before men. T~1ey can leave ~ll their failiugs to the general' mercy of o'od. 8. Unnghteo1um,,u kading to destn1,ction. ." For them that are perishing." From unrighteousness there is a necessary, though, it may not be, an immediate, trnnsition to destruction. When 11:1en d? not observe the rul~s whi_ch are laid down for them by God, they are contendmg with God, and, contendmg with God, they cannot in the end eucceed; for Go~ is stro~1ger than they. There we;e those who were perishing in their unnghteousness In Pauls day. And there are sl1ll those who seem to be perishina in their unrighteousness. 4. TM just dealing of God. (1) What those who are 1~ the antichristian movement n:fect. "Because th~y received not the love of the truth that they might be saved." The apostle holds that it was their own fault if they were perishing. And, in doing so, he brings forward very precious truth. God has in view our salvation. He willeth that all men should be saved, and come to the knowledge of the truth. For this end :he makes us the offer, not of the truth, but Jf the disposition which is necessary for finding it-the love of the truth. Of all .iispositions it is that which is most needed to begin with. It is that which is needed against the <leceitfulness of the heart. It is that which is needed aaainst th deiusi ,·e lies of Satan. If we accept of the love of the truth, if we have th; dis- position to know the truth about ourselves, and to follow the Divine leading-and 3-oci promises us this disposition-then we shall certainly be led on to salvation. But if ~< de not accept of the love of the truth, if we have the disposition to flatt.er ourselves, ani tc: follow some ignisfatuw of our own imagination-and that is only too natural to uF- w• shall as cert~inly be led on to destruction. (2) What they induce. "And for 1hl£ cause God sendeth tl,em a working of error, that they should believe a lie: that they all might be judged who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in righteousness." lleceiving not the truth, it was not with them as though the offer had not been made to them. There was induced a state of judicial blindness. As it was induced in connection with the Divine offer which was refused, and in accordance with the Divine laws in their nature, it could be attributed to God. It could be said that God sent them a working of error, that they should believe a lie. Christianity is the most reasonable, most beautiful thing in existence. But when men are in a state of judicial blindness, they do not see its reasonableness and beauty ; they believe men who lie a.bout it, and treat it with indifference, or disdain, or hatred. This can only lead on to their being judged and condemned, the ground of their condemnation being their not believing the truth especially about Christ, but taking pleasure in unrighteousness. Let us see, then, that we accept the great offer from God of veracity, of love for the truth. Let llll be willing to take a truthful view of things; not taking darkness for light, and evil for good. Let us be willing to follow the Divine leading. Let us especially be open toward Christ-toward the efficacy of his blood, toward the convincing power of his teachings, toward the enjoyment of his fellowship. And, if the antichristia.n manifestation goes forward a.round us, let us be all the more decided on the side of Christ.-R. F.

entries.title: 2TH 2:13–17
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content:
-Exhortation to suadfastne.. I. How GROUNDED. 1. The election ef tAe Theualoniafie. "But we are bound to give thanks to God al way for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, for that God chose you from the beginning unto salvation." This is another overflowing of gratitude for the Thessalonians, who are described not, as in 1 Theas. i. 4, 88 "brethren beloved of God," but 88 u brethren beloved of the Lord," i.e. ~haring with Paul and his colleagues in the special love and care of him who presides over the brotherhood. There is the same inward binding that there waR before (eh. i. 3) to give thanks to God, and to give thanks to God al way. What gave perpetual matttJT of thanksgiving, as in 1 Thess. i. 4, was the election of the Thessalonians. There is not brought in here, as there is there, their being chosen out of a condition of sin, but it is iwplied in their being chos,·11 uuto a oondition of salvation. Thev had been chosen from oe. u. 1-17.) THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANB. 43

the beginning, i.e. from eternity. When God contemplated the creation or 11, race of men, and contemplated at the same time the incursion or evil into human nature and human history, be also contemplated human salvation. It was also within the Divine plnn (going out into all particulars) that the Tbessalonians among others should be saverl. 2. llleans of the realization of their election. (1) Inward means. (a) From the Spirit. "In sanctification of the Spirit." Precedence is naturally given to the work of the Spirit. l<'or we must feel that, if God had not approached ~ first, we never should have npproacbed him. The work of the Spirit, from beginning to end, is a work of sanclification. It is a saving work, inasmuch as it is the reclamation or our nature from unholy uses. On the positive side it is the fitting our nature for Divine uses. As the Spirit is the Agent of our sanctification, his all-sufficient help must be entirely depended upon. (b) From themselve.~. "And belief of the truth." lo election we are responsible for our state of mind. The Spirit works on our mind through the truth. We may think of the truth that God has provided salvation for us. We may also think of the truth that God (according to ver. 10) has made us the offer of the love of the truth. We may further think of the Divine ideal to which our life is to be brought up. The Spirit has aovereign power in the presentation of truth to the mind; and what we have to do is to be receptive, to offer no obstacle to his presentation of the truth. And we are sanctified only in so far as we have received the truth into us. (2) Outward means. "Whereunto he called you through our gosprl." The gospel is especially the offer of salvation on the ground of Christ's death. It was their gospel, as that in connection with which they served God. There was Divine sovereignty in the Thessalonians being favoured with the g"s. el. It wa.s by circumstances over which they had no control that Paul and Silas and TimothJ were sent to Thessalonica. These servants of Christ stood forward and preached the gospel to them, and it was when they received it as a message from God that they were called to salvation. From that point their calling dated. There is added lhe outward aspect of the salvation to which they were called. "To the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ." This is characteristic of the Epistle. The glory tu which we are called is the glory which is possessed by Christ, and which he, as sovereign Dispenser, is to make our possession. We are to be glorified with nothing less than the glory of Christ. It ,vill be seen that God, in electing, has in contemplation all the means of the election being realized. We may assure ourselves of belonging to the number of the elect, in so far as we have evidence of our election in our sanctification. II. How PUT. "S,, then, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye were taught, whether by word, or Epistle of ours." Election contemplating the means of its realization in faith, it is not improper to found upon election an exhortation to steadfastness. They had taken up their Christinn position. Attempts would be made in the way of persecution to move them away from thl'ir position. The ill-grounded expectation of the immediate coming was fraught with perils to them. It was already having a bad effect upon some in making them idle. It would be trying, to think that it was well grounded and not to have it realized. It would even be trying, to know that it was ill grounded and to have to give it up. There would be danger of religious excitement being followed by reaction. Let them beware, then, of apostatizing; let them stand fast. The way in which they were to stand fast was by holding fast the traditions. By the "traditions" we are to understand the truths handed to men. For instance, there was the revelation which was necessary for the stablishing of the The.ssalonians, that there was to be an apostasy before the coming of Christ. In the traditions they bad been instructed both orally and by writing. We are limited to the latter mode of instruction.. Whnt o.re known as ecclesiastical traditions have not independent authority, but have to be tested by the written Word. All our oral instruction has to be founded upon the written Word. Ry being in writing, the truths banded to us are preserved from corruption. We know that we have them in the form in which God wishes us to have them. It is difficult to escape the influence of traditional interpretation. Yet there is always the opp~rtunity of a true interpretation, while we have the text as it wo.s left by inspired men. The written Word is one of the great boons conferred on men. It is a great advanta;.:e to a child that he has not everything to learn for himself, but bas the benefit of the experience of his parents. « THE SECOND EPlSTLE TO THE 'l'HESSALONIANS. [cu. 11, 1-17.

So it is a great advantage to us, that we are not left to our own childish and foolish thoughts, but that we have the written instructions of our heavenly Father. It is by holding to these written instructions, as an unchanging element iu tho midst of all the tests to which we nre subjected, in the •ni<lst or all the temptations to which we are exposed, that we shall be l'nabl,·d valiantly to maintain our Christian position. Ill. How FOLLOWED UP. Invoc,ition qf the Divine blessing. 1. How God is invoked. (1) In the Second Person. "Now our Lord Jesus Christ himself." From evangelical activity there is a rise first to the Mediator and lordly Dispenser of blessings in the Church. After the preachers have done their best for the 'l'hessalonians, they havo the painful consciousness left that they are impotent in themsch•cs, At Corinth Paul plante<l, Apolios watered, but God gave the increase. So Paul and Silas and Timothy feeling tl,at they, in speaking and writing to the Thessalonians, were only held by hi0:: who holds the seven stars in his right hand, implore his help to make their activity ~uccessful. "Our Lord Jesus Christ himself accomplish what we are aimina at for them. Let his almighty efficacy be communicated through our feeble instrumettality.• If we would do any good to any in whom we are interested, Christ must do it for us. His high priestly service must be recognized by us. Therefore let us ever rise above our mere wishing an<l striving for others to him who can make our wishing and striving effectual. (2) In the First Person. (a) His fatl,erhood. "And God our Father." From evangelical activity there is a rise, through the Mediator, to him who is the Final Reason and Contriver of redemption. We have some influence with God when we can call him onr Father. We naturally expect to have more influence with a friend than with a stranger. We can appeal to him as a friend. We can; if need be, intercede on the score of friendship and long acquaintance. So we can appeal to God as our Father, to bless not only ourselves but others. And, should every other appeal fail, surel_\' this shall not fail. When the cry comes up on behalf of his needy children, "Our Father, wilt thou not bless?" surely he will not turn away his ear. (b) Wherein it was manifested. "Which loved us." This is timed in the past, and calls up the great act of love-the gift of the Son. Our Father, who gave his Son for us. We can behold in this how GPd can love. Some would represent it as very un- fatherly. But, apart from tbe Sou's unforced consent, there is this consideration, that, where there is true fatherly feeling, it is not more easy to sacrifice a son than to sacrifice one's self. David felt this when be uttered his lamentation over Absalom: "Would God I had died for thee, 0 Absalom, my son, my son I" We must hold that, loving the Soo infinitely, the Father could as well have sacrificed himself as his Son. The marvel and mystery is, that, loving his Son infinitely, he could be moved to sacrifice him for us bis undeserving creatures. But surely by this act of devotion the love of God for us is placed fur ever beyond all doubt. In presence of the cross, to doubt, or to act as though we doubted, tbat God loves us, is doing him the most glaring injustice. (c) What it obtained for us. "And gave us eternal comfort." There is no hiding it, that it is comfort that we all need. There is an evil heart, to keep us from being happy. It gives rise to slavish fear of God and forebodings of judgment. There is ali!o an evil world, which alone is sufficient to keep us from being perfectly happy. It is an evil world, where there is exposure to poverty, to sickness, to bereavement, to <leath. It is an evil world, where, with sensitive spirits, we have to look forth on so much sin and wretchedness. Where, then, is the comfort? There is no real comfort for a guilty conscience in ignorance or distraction. It is unsubstantial comfort, to know that our suffering is common. There is some substantial comfort in the sympathy of our fellow-men, but it is variable. We may not find friends all that we would desire them to be to us. Those by whom we are most comforted may be taken away, and we have to be comforted for their loss. But there is comfort provided by eternal love, and comfort that is eternal in its nature. There is comfort in knowing that our great Substitute has made full salisl'action for our sin. There iB comfort in knowing that we are clasped to the heart of the eve~lastlng Father. That is comfort which is neither deceitful nor fleeting. It is sufficient for us amid all the cares of life. It is independent of all contingencies. "And good hope." Comfort refers to time present; hope refer11 to time future. Beyond all that we have of good and of coml'ort under evil, there is hope. And what is this hope? ft is the hope of our real joys being perfected, of our being delivered from the plague 011. n. 1-17.] 'fHE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS. 46

of an evil hflart and the burden of an evil world, of our being placed where there will be no more need of comfort-in the presence of the eternal Love. It is also a good hope, in its being well founrleJ-not founded on our own thoughts, but founded on ~he. charnct~r a~d work and promise of God. It is a. hope ,~hich ie even now good m 1te cheermg influence upon our hearts. (a) Obtained without deserving of oors. "Through grace." The comfort is not self-created ; we have had nothing to do with the procuring of it. But, seeing it has been graciously provided for ue by eternal Love, we have good reason for taking it in the whole benefit into our hearts. The hope is one which we could not have dared to cherish of ourselves. It is far beyond anything that we could have thought of. But we cannot limit the grace of God. If it is his good pleasure to give us this hope, we have good reason for cherishing it. 2. For what end God is invoked.. (1) To bless the Th,ssalonians with romfort. "Comfort your hearts." There is another incidental proof hero of the Divinity of our Lord in the use of a singular verb, while both our Lord Jesus Christ and God our Father are the subject. 'l.'he hearts of the Thessalonians were full of hopes and feal'II in view of the coming which was thought to be imminent; comfort is, therefore, invoked for their hearts. It cannot but be congeniAI to God to comfort the Church. "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God. Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warrare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned: for she bath received of the Lord's hand double for all her sins." Having provided the comfort in Christ, he must best know how, through Christ, to apply it to our need. (2) To bless them also with stability. "And stablish them." Comfort is invoked partly with a view to stability. When we are uncomforted we are unstable as water. Our energies are relaxed, and we are unfitted for our work. Sorrow is weakness, but comfort is strength. Double sphere in which stability is invoked/or them. (a) Work. "In every good work." It was not unnecessary that they should be reminded that they were called to work, even to work with their bands. God gra.nt them all the good elements which belong to work. Let the simplest work be done honestly. Let not their works " with self be soiled." Let them be done unto the glory of God. In these, and in all the elements of good work, let them be confirmed. (b) Word. "And word." Good speaking is even more difficult than good acting. "If any man offend not in wo~d, the same is a perfect man." God grant them all the good elements which belong to speaking. Let every word be characterized by truthfulness. Let it also have fitness; for "a won! fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver." Let it also have wholesomeness, and not be like bad frnit. Let it breathe kindliness. Let it breathe loyalty to Christ. In these, and in all 1ne elements of good speaking, let them be confirmed.-R. F. Vel'll. 1, 2.-.4 great delusion. One object, perhaps the principal object, of this Second Epistle to the Tbcssalonians, following as it does so closely upon the First Epistle, is to correct a disturbing error that was obtaining some considerable footing among the Macedonian Christians. I. THE GBEAT DELUSION. The First Epistle contains repeated references to llD. expectation of the second advent of Christ which was evidently very strong in the Thessalonian Church. The wish is father to the thought. From expecting "the day of the Lord" to arrive at any moment, some bad beeb led, on most insufficient evidence, to ask whether it had not already come. The great delusion was that "the day of the Lord is now present." It is not likely that any supposed Christ to have come, though in an invisible way, and in a different manner from which it was expected, or that they thought be might have co::ne to another place, unseen 1rnd unknown to the Churches of northern Greece. What they were inclined to think seems to have been that the new era in which Christ was to appear h11d already dawned, though he himself had not yet come. Similar is the delusion of auy who suppose that the day of grace is over and the time of judgment come, or that of those who think they have got into a new dispensation beyond the dispt·nsation of the New Testament. II. THE souR0ll:8 01' THE llELUSlON. 1. Latter-day prophecy. The expression "either by spirit" seems to refer to the supposed inspiration of Christian prophets. St. Paul had previously warned his friends to prove all things, while not quenching the Spirit by despising prophesyings (1 Thess. v. 19-21). We must beware of self- 46 TUE SECOND EPISTLE 'l'O THE THESSALONIANS. [ea, 11. 1-17,

deluded fanRtics as well as of deliberate deceivers. 2. False apostoltcal tradititm. " By word" probably menns by repnrt,,d word of St. Paul, which word, however, never really came from him. Thus early were false traditions afloat. See the mistalten tradition about St. John (John xxi. 23). If these erroneous traditions were current during the lifetime of the apostles, how can we accept so-called "apostolic tradition" as an authority? 3. A forged Epistle. The mistake could scarcely have arisen from our First Epistle to the Thessalonians, since that Epistle referred to the great day as future, while the error made it present. It is important to ascertain the authenticity of the books of Scripture. III. THE DANGER OF THE DELUBION. St. Paul warns against it as something to be c:arefully avoided. Many evils attached to it. 1. Erroneow views. These are bad in themselves, as true Yiews are desirable on their own account. The soul suffers for want of truth as the body for want of light. 2. Dishonouring conceptions of the second advent. If the day were already come, where was the glory, the judgment, the rectification of all things? False doctrines dishonour Christ even when they are meant to glorify him. 3. ConfU$ion of conduct. Such a delusion as that which was creeping into the Tiies~r1lonian Church would disarrange all practical life. Delusions about the IICCOnd advent distract attention from sober Christian work. IV. THE WAR~'"ING AGAINST THE DELUSION. 1. Form no hasty opinion. "Be not quickly shaken," etc. Specious arguments should be examined at leisure before they are adopted. 2. Do ,a.ot permit novel teaching lo give distress. If the heart is well settled in Christian truth, though the mind should be open to receive new light, no distress or disturbance need be felt. 3. Beware of deception. "Let no man beguile you." Christians should be watchful and " wise as serpeats," each having his own independent convictions.-W. F. A.

entries.title: 2TH 2:3
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content:
-The man of sin. The man of sin and his awful character and career, here described by St. Paul, are subjects of such deep and dreadful mystery, that we may well take warning from the intricate confusion of the interpretations put forth by those people who profess to exponnd the fulfilment of prophecy, and content ourselves with accepting the prediction as it stands without attempting to identify it with particular historical events. Though some of its terms apply well to certain explanations, and others to different explanations, no explanation has yet been furnished which fairly and without any straining of words covers the whole of them. From Nero to the pope, from the days of the siege of Jerusalem to those of the yet future millennium, certain odioua persons and systems have been selected for a realization of the prophecy, Leaving these dubious identifications, let ns look at the main outlines of the picture. L THERE IS A HAN OF BIN. Whether he lived in the past or has yet to appear, a man to whom this awful name belongs is described in inspired Scripture. The Bible does not ignore the awful depths of human wickedness. It is dreadfully siguificant that this evil beina is a man, not a deviL Humanity, which was created in the image of God and intend~d to be a temple of God, may be degraded into the image of Sa.tan and become a haunt of iniquity. As good works through humau sympathies, so does evil. A bad man is more dangeroue than a fallen angel, because he is nearer to his fellow-men. II. THB llAl!l OF SIN FOLLOW~ All APOSTASY, 1. Spiritual apostasy leads a man to moral rm-ruption. The man who has forsaken Christ is tempted to fall into gross sin. Faith is the great preservative of morals. 2. .,tJ,postasy lays the Ohurch open to attacks from her 1memies. The "man of sin" could not arise before the Church had fallen, nor if he had ap1,eared could he have had any power against a faithful Church, IIL THE MAK OF SIN PRECEDES THE SECOND ADVENT OF CBBIST. It was a mistake on the part of the Thessalonian Church to suppose tLat "the day of the Lord" had arrived, because the dreadful appearance of the man of sin which was to precede that day had not yet been seen. St. Paul warns us that apostasy and the frightful life of thi.11 wicked man-whoever he may be--must come before Christ returns, He does not encourage ue to look for a gradual, unbroken progress of Christianity. The growth of the harvest fruit is arrested and delayed by frost and storm. Christ even wondered whether he should find any faith left on the earth at his return (Luke xviiL 8). The glorioua consummation of all things to which the Christian looks forward is not to be oe. 11. 1-17.) THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS. f7

expected ae the reeult of \uiet improvement wit.hout relapse. Between the preeent and that" great Divine event dark chasms of iniquity yawn. Every age bas thought it could detect signs of this evil in its midst. So the unbelief and corruptions of our own day are taken by some to be "signs." Unhappily the language of the apo8'le warne us to expect more terribly demonstrative signs than any yet seen. IV, THE APPEARANCE OF THE MAN OF SIN 18 A SIGN OJI' THE APPROACHING ADVENT OJI' OHRIST. Here ie some encouragement for the Ch11rch to endure the trials of the darkest times. 'l'hese times are to usher in the ii;reat and glorious day of the Lord. Evil, when most triumphant, is nearest defeat. Dreadful as may be its transient success, it will soon be swept away. When the horror of sin is blackest, the jud6rment which is to sweep it away ie nearest at hand. Christ will come again when be will be most needed. -W.F.A.

entries.title: 2TH 2:7
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content: -7'ul mystery of lawlessness. The exact, objective application of this prediction, like that of the preceding description, is not easy to discover. But principles are involved which are susceptible of general application. 1. THERE 18 A MYSTERY OF LAWLESSNESS. By this expression the apostle probably means a mystery the character of which is lawless. 1. We may e:rpect to meet with new mysteries. ~hile time and inquiry resolve some mysteries, they bring upon us fresh ones. We are not to expect to be able to understand all the forces and influences with which we are surrounded. It is enough that we are in the hands of God who knows all, and trusting in Christ who can lead us safely through the darkness. 2. New mysteries may be characterized 1Yy new lawlessness. The answer to our inquiries may be very unsatisfactory in revealing only evil. There are strange novelties which are obscure in all points but their moral character, and that is plainly evil. If so, we may hope for no good from them, and need not further interest ourselves in them. 3. .dll lawlessness i, mysterious. How did it originate? How is its existence possible? Why does not God sweep it away? These questions have perplexed men in all ages. We bow before them in helpless, pained wonder. Il. THERE 18 A RESTRAINT ON THE MYSTERY OP LAWLESSNESS, 1. Ila f'l/,ll power is not yet revealed. There are those who treat all sin with unbecoming levity, because they do not yet see its terrible fruits. They are playing with a torpid adder, that may awake at any moment and inflict a fatal wound. No one knows what bidden posaibilities of harm lurk in the deep caverns of undeveloped sin. There are volcanoes iu the hearts of some quiet men which may burst into destructive fires. 2. H'l/,man means may be used to restrain the mystery of lawlessness. Government, law, society, healthy habits of the majority, keep it down for a time. 3. God holds the mystery of lawlessness in check. He is supreme over its wildest raging. " He that sittetb in the heavens shall laugh." God restrains the superabundant wrath of man (Ps. lxxvi. 10). Ill. THE HIDDEN MYSTERY OF LAWLESSNESS WILL BE BEVEALED. The volcano must break into eruption some day. Evil cannot slumber for ever. Hypocrisy will tire of its meek, innocent demeanour. The harvest of sin will have to be reaped. Let not any man put his confidence in the secretness or slowness of the processes of evil. The more they are hidden now, the worse will be the appalling outburst of them when the restraint under which they groan at present is released. The longer the wild horses are held in by the leash, the fiercer will be their mad gallop when they break loose. IV. CHRIST WILL CONQUER THE MYSTERY OF LAWLESSNESS. Evil will not long be rampant. One fearful rebellion and then a tremendous defeat. 1. Christ i, to be the Oonq'UIJror of it. He came to destroy the works of the devil. We could not effect this great work, He, our Saviour, does it for us. 2. (,'hrist is to come ugain for this object. When the mystery is revealed, Christ's " manifestation " follows. 3. Christ conq'l/,erS with a breath. His first work was difficult, involving bis death. His la.st work will be divinely simple, and yet sublimely successfu!.-W. F. A.

entries.title: 2TH 2:10–12
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content:
-The love of the truth. The reason for the doom of those who are to be destroyed at Uie 1econd coming of Christ here given, is that they do not receive the love of the truth. I, GOD EXPECTS US 'l'O IU!:OEIVB TSE LOVE OF THE TRUTH, I. Truth ii gooa in i8 'l'HE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIAr-;s [cu. II, 1-17.

itstlf. Truth is to the soul what light ls to the body. It is natural for men to love the day, unnatural for them to shun it. In a right and healthy state we should love truth simply as truth, whatever else it be. 2. Christian trnth is peculiai·ly attmctiuc. Scientific truth is beautiful, philosophic truth is valuable; but the truth of the crospel has far deeper attractions, because it contains revelation of the love and fatherh~ of God, of the grace and goodness of Christ, of the redemption of the world, of the way of alvation, of the heavenly rest, et.o. S. Truth slumld be welcomed with love. We cannot accept it to any a,lvantage until we love it; for (1) love opens our eyes to a sympa- thetic under:;tanding of it, and (2) love saves us from a cold, barren acceptance of it, and helps us to receive it profitably. II. IT 16 AN EVIL HEART THAT PBEVE1''TS MEN FROM RECEIVING THB LOVB OF THB TBtJTB. St. Paul traces back the bad condition of those who reject the love of the truth to the fact that they "had pleasure in unrighteousness." 'l'he pleasures of sin cannot exist side by side with the love of the truth. Evil hates the light (John iii. 19). Moral corruption has no sympathy for the lofty thirst for truth of a pure soul. Hence it may be concluded that indifference to truth is a sign of moral evil. The corrupt life is a false life, and its departure from truth reveals the baseness of the character beneath. This is why the rejection of the truth is culpable. Intellectual doubt is of quite a different character. Indeed, it often arises from genuine love of truth, while self-satisfied orthodoxy is often quite indifferent to verifiable facts, preferring respectable error to painful truth. II!. THE PENALTY OF REJECTING THB LOVB. OF THB TRUTH IS INCAPACITY TO KNOW TRUTH FROM ERROR. God punishes men in this condition by sending "them a working of error, that t.hey should believe a lie." This is an awful fate. Truth is too precious a pearl to be cast before swine. They who do not love it shall not have it. Liars become incapable of knowing truth. The habit of indifference to truth so grows upon some people that the whole idea of truth becomes obscure and meaningless to them, and they ask with Pi late, half bewildered, half scornful, "What is truth?" Is not this a veritable destruction-the spiritual eye blinded and burnt out by the fires of falsehood and unrighteousness; the highest intellectual faculty, that of grasping truth, killed by C01Tuption and falsehood? God save us all from this hideous doom 1:- W. F. A.

entries.title: 2TH 2:13
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content:
-The Divine work of salvation. We are to be thankful to God for the happy spiritual prospects of our fellow-Christians, because they all ~pring from hie good purpose and work. The most striking characteristic of the description before us is its attributing the whole process from beginning to end to the will and action of God. L THI: BEGINNING. 1. .fo initial Divine choice. This dates back to the dim ages of an awful antiquity. In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. In the beginning was the Word. In the beginning God chose his people for himself. Salvation is no after-thought coming in to redeem the failure of creation. It was all planned from the first. When God ma.de man he foresaw sin and determined on redemption. Each one of us is thought of by God from the first. We come into the world to fulfil vocations which God designed for us wh1;n he first planned the universe. 2. .A present Divine call. The choice would be of no use if it were not rna<le known to us. But when the time for executing God's great design has arrived, he makes it sufficiently known for us to be able to follow it. He calls by the preaching of the gospel. The gospel, then, ill an invitation. It is ~ood news, but only for those who will accept the invitation. Thill new gospel came to bid men fulfil an ancient destiny. 'l'he late_st work accomplishes the oldest thought of God. II. 'IRE PBOCEl!8. 1. Sanctijkation of the Spi,rit. This is the Divine side of the process. Prior to it is the great atoning work of Christ. But that work is done for us that we may receive the Spirit of God as its fruit. Now we are looking at the work of God in us. God purifies and consecrates his people by an inspiration of his own Spirit. No safety is possible to the guilty, no glory to the unholy. 'l'he cleansing process must come before the great end can be reached. 2. Belief of the truth. This u our side of the proceBB. It is useless for us to wait for our sanctification and for the baptism of the Holy Sl'irit which ill to produce it. It will not come without our active reception of it. There is oo magic about the process of the dP.ecent of the Holy Ghost. on. 11. 1-17.J THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS. '9

J t comes on certain conditions being fulfilled by us. (1) 7'ruth is the vehicle that con~eys. it into our hearts. (2) Faith is the door ID our hearts that opens to receive 1t. III. THE Y.ND. 1. Salvation. Take this word in the largest, roundest sense, u deliverance from all evil. It is painfully true that in our greatest joy e.nd thankfulneRs we have to recollect that e.t best we are plucked as brands from the burning. No blessing ce.n be enjoyed till the awful ruin into which our souls were all of them sinking through our great and dreadful sin has been stayed. 2. Glqry. Balntion is the bei,:inning of God's work in us; glory is the completion of it. We ce.n have no glory while we are in the mire of sin and wretchedness. But when we a.re delivered, God will not leave us like drowning men on a barren rock, saved from present destruction indeed, but with dreary future prospects. He will not have ended his work with us till he has exalted us into the region of his own glory.-W. F. A.

entries.title: 2TH 2:16
entries.author: Paton James Gloag
entries.content:
-.A benediction. I. THE BOUBCEB OJ' THE BENEDICTION. A true benediction is more than an expression of good wishes. It is a prayer by one who has especial weight in intercession, although it is expressed to the person for whom it is offered. The benediction of so great and good a man as St. Paul is of great value, because the "effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.n But the blessings desired by the apostle are not given by him any more than the blessings of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to their children were given by the patriarchs. The sources of the blessings of a benediction are not human nor earthly at all. Here they are declared. 1. The personal influence of Jesus O'hrist. This is strikingly expressed by the reference to "our Lord Jesus Christ himself." His brotherhood and his love lead him to bless us. His Divinity, his goodness, and his sacrifice give him authority in heaven. In his own right he blesses. And he does not delegate the blessing. He confers it himself. 2. The fatherhood of God. Because God is "our Father n we may expect blessings from him. Fears and doubts arise from partial views of God, and views which leave out of account his great fatherly nature. He does not bless as a Master paying wages, but as a Father dealing affectionately with his children. II. THE ASSURANCES OF THE BKNEDICTION. Grounds for believing that God will give the blessing are given for the encouragement of faith. 1. Love in the past. H11 has revealed his character by his providence, and he has proved in this way that he loves his children. But a parent's love is distinguished from all other kinds of love by its permanence. If God ever did love, he still lovea. 2. Eternal comfort. This we have now in the peace of forgiveness and the rest of faith. The peace is such that the world can neither give nor take away. The rest is beneath the shadow of a great rock that outlasts even the seemingly everlasting hills. 3. Hope for the future. God has uttered promises and encouraged hopes. We cannot believe that he will mock the expectations which he has raised. III. 'THE OBJECTS OF 1'RE BENEDICTION. 1. Heart-comfort. We have eternal comfort; nevertheless we need more comfort. No soul is yet perfectly st rest. Sorrow distresses the most trustful. (1) Observe the breadth of the Divine comfort. We may have it in some departments of life and yet miss it in others. The Greek word paraklesis has a wider, fuller meaning than our word "comfort." It stands for all help, and help in every direction is what our souls need. (2) Note the home of the Divine comfort. It is to he in our hearts. Comfort anywhere else is vain. Comfortable houses, clothes, etc., leave the deepest trouble untouched. The bee.rt may be on a rack when the body is on a downy couch. God's comfort reaches the bee.rt. 2. Stability in work and word. We must not stop at comfort. We are consoled in distress that we may be free and strong and glari for sen·ice. (1) The service must come from the heart. "The heart" is to be stablished for service. (2) It must be various and complete-" every good work." (3) It must extend to speech-" and word." The Scriptures lay great stress on a right use of speech. (4) It must be steadfast. '!'his is the end of the benediction. Eternal comfort must be balanced by steadfast faithfulness.-W. F. A.

'l'hose notions were shaped by the floating belief of his day, and have nothing beyond an historical interest. They belong to the past of Christianity-to its infantine state, when it was emerging out of Judaism, and assuming that independent position to which no man contributed so much as the apostle of the Gen tiles.'
